Represent the final Cartan involution by a positive definite form and rescale its change-of-basis matrix to determinant one.
acceptance: For g = (1 1; 0 1) the torus g·D·g⁻¹ = {(x, y−x; 0, y)} (D diagonal) is not transpose-stable, and a = g⁻¹ ∈ SL_2(ℝ) makes it D. For the non-reductive N = {(1 x; 0 1)} no a works: a transpose-stable unipotent group containing u ≠ 1 would contain the non-unipotent element u·uᵀ.

sources.match: The finite-chain statement is proved by induction from §1.8.

nodes.title: Reductive homogeneous spaces as closed orbits
nodes.statement: If H⊂G are reductive algebraic groups over a characteristic-zero field F, then H\G is affine and has a G-equivariant closed immersion into a finite-dimensional rational G-representation, taking the identity coset to w∈V(F) with stabilizer H. The orbit of w is closed.
hypotheses: F a field of characteristic 0; G a reductive (not necessarily connected) linear algebraic group over F; H ⊂ G a reductive closed F-subgroup
proofSteps: Use the affine homogeneous-space criterion for reductive H requested from RG2.1.
Choose finitely many generators of its affine coordinate algebra; include them in a finite-dimensional G-stable subspace.
Dualize the evaluation embedding. Equivariance identifies the image as the closed orbit, and the stabilizer is H as a group scheme.
acceptance: SL_2 ⊃ N = {(1 x; 0 1)} (not reductive): SL_2/N ≅ 𝔸² ∖ {0} is not affine and the orbit of (0, 1) under right multiplication is not closed. GL_2 ⊃ O(x²+y²): the orbit of q = x²+y² in binary forms is open, not closed; in Sym² ⊕ (det⁻² line) the orbit of (q, 1) is the closed hypersurface disc(f)·t = disc(q), with stabilizer O(q).

sources.match: The affine-space realization supplies the primitive representation; it is distinct from adelic orbit finiteness.

nodes.title: Closed-orbit weight bounds in a real Siegel domain
nodes.statement: Let GL_n act rationally on V, w have closed orbit and transpose-stable stabilizer, and Γ⊂V(ℚ) be a lattice. Let GL_n(ℝ) act on the left and let Σ = ω·A_t·O(n) be a standard real Siegel domain in the left-quotient convention of gln-real-reduction (BHC §5.3 uses the equivalent right action v·g = g⁻¹·v and the inverse domain O(n)·A_t⁻¹·ω⁻¹). There is a compact Q⊂GL_n(ℝ) such that Σ·w∩Γ⊂Q·w. In particular the norms of these lattice points are uniformly bounded.
hypotheses: V a finite-dimensional rational representation of GL_n over ℚ; w ∈ V(ℝ) with closed GL_n(ℂ)-orbit and transpose-stable stabilizer in GL_n(ℝ); Γ ⊂ V(ℚ) a lattice; Σ a standard Siegel domain for the upper triangular Borel and O(n)
proofSteps: Diagonalize the rational split-torus action into finitely many weight spaces and use that a nonzero coordinate in the fixed lattice is bounded away from zero.
Borel–Harish-Chandra §5.3 applies the square-weight estimate to replace a Siegel-domain representative by one in the stabilizer times a compact set.

Transpose stability gives the second compact bound after applying the Cartan involution; bounded unipotent factors stay bounded under the allowed chamber conjugations. The precise squared-weight estimate and proper orbit map are retained as named missing inputs.
acceptance: GL_2 acting on Sym² ⊕ ℝ by g·(F, t) = (gFgᵀ, det(g)⁻²t), w = (I, 1), Γ = Sym²(ℤ) ⊕ ℤ: the orbit det(F)·t = 1 is closed with stabilizer O(2), and Σ·w ∩ Γ consists of the (n a²nᵀ, 1) of determinant 1 with 1 ≤ a_2² ≤ 1/t, a finite set. With the right action F ↦ XᵀFX and the same Σ, every form (m²+1, m; m, 1) is hit, so finiteness fails.

sources.match: The weight-bound lemma is the primitive step used by lattice finiteness.

nodes.title: Closed-orbit lattice finiteness
nodes.statement: Under closed-orbit-weight-bound, Σ·w∩Γ is finite. The same holds for any other lattice of V(ℚ), in particular after replacing Σ by c·Σ for fixed c ∈ GL_n(ℚ), since c·Σ·w∩Γ = c·(Σ·w∩c⁻¹Γ).
hypotheses: the hypotheses of closed-orbit-weight-bound (rational GL_n-representation V over ℚ, w ∈ V(ℝ) with closed orbit and transpose-stable stabilizer, Γ ⊂ V(ℚ) a lattice, Σ a left-convention standard Siegel domain)
proofSteps: The weight-bound puts the intersection in a compact subset of V.
The lattice is discrete, so its intersection with that compact set is finite.
A rational matrix maps a rational lattice to a rational lattice, so the left translate c·Σ reduces to the lattice c⁻¹Γ with the same w and stabilizer.
acceptance: For the GL_2 example of closed-orbit-weight-bound with w = (I, 1) the intersection is the finite set of reduced integral binary forms of determinant 1 (with t = 1); for SL_2 acting on forms of determinant −1 (signature (1,1)) the corresponding reduced integral forms are also finitely many (BHC 5.5).

sources.match: Discreteness completes the independent weight estimate.

nodes.title: Compact finite parts give bounded denominators
nodes.statement: For a rational representation ρ:G→GL(V), w∈V(F) and compact C⊂G(𝔸_f), there is a fractional O_F-lattice L⊂V(F) such that wρ(C)∩V(F)⊂L. Likewise a compact C bounds denominators of all entries of g and g⁻¹ for g∈C∩GL_n(F).
hypotheses: F a number field; G a linear algebraic group over F with a rational representation ρ: G → GL(V) over F; w ∈ V(F); C ⊂ G(𝔸_{F,f}) compact (for the second claim G = GL_n and ρ the identity)
proofSteps: Cover the compact set by finitely many restricted-product boxes.
Only finitely many places allow denominators, and compactness bounds each valuation below there.
Intersect these valuation bounds with V(F); the result is a fractional lattice.
acceptance: G = GL_1 = V over ℚ, w = 1, C = p⁻¹ℤ_p^× × ∏_{ℓ≠p} ℤ_ℓ^×: C ∩ ℚ = {±1/p} ⊂ p⁻¹ℤ. For the closed noncompact set C = 𝔸_f^× the intersection is all of ℚ^×, contained in no fractional lattice.

sources.match: The adelic lift of real finiteness uses bounded denominators.

nodes.title: Real GLₙ Siegel overlap
nodes.statement: For a standard GL_n(ℝ) Siegel domain Σ and a fixed integer d≥1, the set of γ∈GL_n(ℚ) with γ,γ⁻¹∈d^−1M_n(ℤ) and γΣ∩Σ≠∅ is finite. The same statement holds for two fixed rational translates of such domains.
hypotheses: n ≥ 1; d ≥ 1 an integer; Σ a standard Siegel domain of GL_n(ℝ) in the left-quotient convention of gln-real-reduction; for the second claim c_1, c_2 ∈ GL_n(ℚ) fixed and the overlap condition γc_1Σ ∩ c_2Σ ≠ ∅
proofSteps: Use the classical real Siegel property for bounded-denominator arithmetic lattices (Borel §3.3 and Borel–Harish-Chandra §4.5).
Conjugate fixed rational translates and enlarge the denominator bound.
The general-dimensional Siegel estimate is a recorded primitive input; the Mathlib SL₂ modular-domain theorem supplies only a special-case test.
acceptance: n = 1: Σ = ℝ^× meets γΣ for every γ ∈ ℚ^×; the γ with γ, γ⁻¹ ∈ d⁻¹ℤ are ±m/d with m | d² (only ±1 for d = 1), a finite set, whereas without the denominator bound all of ℚ^× qualifies.

sources.match: §3.1: the finiteness condition is unchanged when the arithmetic element may have bounded denominators, because only finitely many lattices lie between two given lattices; §3.3: Siegel's theorem gives this condition for the standard GL_n(ℝ) domain (right-quotient form; inverted here).

nodes.title: Local polynomial comparison for algebraic heights
nodes.statement: For closed algebraic embeddings σ,τ of an affine group G into general linear groups and dual-augmented norms, there are integers N≥1 and positive c_v, with c_v=1 at almost all finite places, such that ‖τ(g)‖_v≤c_v‖σ(g)‖_v^N. The statement includes inverse coordinates.
hypotheses: F a number field; G an affine algebraic group over F; σ: G → GL_m and τ: G → GL_{m′} closed immersions over F; local norms as in adelic-height applied to σ ⊕ σ^∨ and τ ⊕ τ^∨
proofSteps: The coordinate algebra is generated by the σ matrix and inverse matrix entries, so each τ and inverse τ coefficient is a polynomial in them.
At finite places use the ultrametric maximum bound; the polynomial coefficients and integral models are units outside finitely many places.
At real/complex places sum the finitely many monomial bounds, respecting the square absolute value at complex places.
acceptance: G_m over ℚ, σ(x) = x, τ(x) = diag(x, x²): with duals ‖τ(x)‖_p = max(|x|_p, |x|_p⁻¹)² = ‖σ(x)‖_p² (c_p = 1) and ‖τ(x)‖_∞ = √(x²+x⁴+x⁻²+x⁻⁴) ≤ √2·(x²+x⁻²) = √2‖σ(x)‖_∞² (N = 2). Without dual summands |x_∞| bounds no power of the coordinate x⁻¹ as x → 0.

sources.match: Local norms on GL(m) (maximum at p-adic places, Hilbert–Schmidt at ∞) and the height through a rational embedding r with polynomial inverse bound; the comparison of two embeddings is not proved there.

nodes.title: Properness of dual-augmented adelic height
nodes.statement: If r contains a closed embedding σ and σ∨, the product height in adelic-height has compact sublevel sets. At infinity it bounds both σ(g) and σ(g)⁻¹; at finite v its value is ≥1 and, when not integral in both directions, is ≥q_v. A height bound therefore allows only finitely many exceptional finite places.
hypotheses: F a number field; G an affine algebraic group over F; σ: G → GL_n a closed immersion over F; r contains σ ⊕ σ^∨; local norms normalized as in adelic-height
proofSteps: The matrix and inverse-matrix bounds form a compact subset of GL_n(F_v) at each exceptional place.
Only the finitely many v with q_v≤R can have local norm>1 on a height-R sublevel set; at all others the point lies in the fixed integral subgroup.
Take the resulting finite-level compact product and intersect the closed sublevel set, using the closed embedding topology.
acceptance: G_m over ℚ with r = id ⊕ dual: ‖x‖ ≤ R forces R⁻¹ ≤ |x_∞| ≤ R, p^{|v_p(x_p)|} ≤ R for every p (so x_p ∈ ℤ_p^× when p > R): a compact set. With r = id the height is the idele norm, whose sublevel set {|x| ≤ 1} contains 𝔸^1 and is not compact.

sources.match: Asserts that r can be chosen so that height balls in G(𝔸) are compact; that the dual summand provides this is the packet's argument.

nodes.title: Polynomial count of rational coordinates
nodes.statement: For a fixed number field F and integer d≥1, the number of a∈F^d with ∏_v max(1,|a₁|_v,…,|a_d|_v)≤R is at most C R^N for R≥1, for constants C,N depending only on F,d. The absolute values are normalized for the product formula.
hypotheses: F a number field; d ≥ 1; absolute values normalized for the product formula (|·|_v = |·|^{[F_v:ℝ]} at archimedean v); R ≥ 1
proofSteps: Clear the denominator ideal and sort vectors by the corresponding ideal norm, which is bounded by a power of R.
Choose ideal-class representatives and rescale by units into a bounded logarithmic fundamental domain.

The archimedean bounds then give a lattice box of polynomial size, while the number of possible denominator ideals is polynomially bounded. Ideal-class finiteness, the unit fundamental domain, ideal counting and lattice-point bounds are retained as exact missing inputs.
acceptance: F = ℚ, d = 1: for a = p/q in lowest terms, ∏_ℓ max(1, |a|_ℓ) = |q|, so the height is max(|p|, |q|) and the count is at most (2R+1)². Dropping the finite places, infinitely many a (e.g. 1/n) satisfy max(1, |a|_∞) ≤ 1.

sources.match: (13.4): the number of rational points of G of height at most t is bounded by a constant times a power of t; stated with a reference to Borel, without proof.

nodes.title: Exponential integrability on the relative chamber
nodes.statement: Let β₁,…,β_r be a basis of (a₀^G)* and let 2ρ=∑c_iβ_i with every c_i>0. For any T the integral of exp(−2ρ(H)) over β_i(H)>β_i(T) is finite. For r=0 the domain is the zero-dimensional point and has the chosen finite Haar mass.
hypotheses: r ≥ 0; a₀^G a real vector space of dimension r with a Haar (Lebesgue) measure; β_1, …, β_r a basis of its dual; c_1, …, c_r > 0 with 2ρ = Σ c_iβ_i; T ∈ a₀^G
proofSteps: Apply the linear coordinate isomorphism H↦(β_i(H)).
The integral is a positive Jacobian constant times ∏∫_{β_i(T)}^∞exp(−c_i t)dt.
Each factor equals exp(−c_iβ_i(T))/c_i; the empty product handles the anisotropic case.
acceptance: SL_2 (r = 1, β = α, 2ρ = α): ∫_{α(H) > t₀} e^{−α(H)} dH = e^{−t₀} in the coordinate t = α(H); with y = e^t this is ∫_{y₀}^∞ dy/y² = 1/y₀, the area of {|x| ≤ 1/2, y > y₀}. With the inverse density e^{+2ρ} (or any c_i ≤ 0) the integral diverges.

sources.match: Definition of Siegel sets and Figure 8.1: the condition β(H_{P0}(a) − T_1) > 0 for β ∈ Δ_0 cuts out the translated cone T_1 + a_{P0}^+ over which the integral is taken; the integral itself is elementary and not in the source.

nodes.title: Scalar invariance of reduced forms
nodes.statement: For a positive definite Gram matrix B, C>0 and a>0, B is (e,C)-reduced iff aB is (e,C)-reduced. Consequently determinant normalization preserves reducedness.
hypotheses: B a positive definite real symmetric n × n matrix (the Gram matrix of b in the basis e); C > 0; a > 0 real
proofSteps: The first two inequalities scale by a; both sides of the determinant inequality scale by a^n.
Positive definiteness is preserved by a>0. Apply a=det(B)^−1/n.
acceptance: diag(1, 4) is (std, 2)-reduced and so is its determinant-one normalization diag(1/2, 2) (1/2 < 1, 2 < 4; 1/2 < 4; 1 < 2·1). The hypothesis a > 0 is needed: −diag(1, 4) fails condition (1) at i = j = 1, since 1 < 2·(−1) is false.

sources.match: Reducedness is defined on the whole cone X of positive definite forms by three conditions, each homogeneous in b; this node records the resulting scalar invariance.

nodes.title: Compatible parabolic and torus for a subgroup
nodes.statement: For H⊂G reductive over ℚ, a Siegel triple (P_H,S_H,K_H), and K_G containing K_H with Cartan involution stabilizing S_H, choose a parabolic ℚ-subgroup Q⊂G with Levi Z_G(S_H) and N_H⊂R_u(Q), then a minimal P_G⊂Q. Its Cartan-stable Siegel torus S_G contains S_H, satisfies S_G∩H=S_H, and N_H⊂N_G.
hypotheses: H ⊂ G reductive ℚ-groups; (P_H, S_H, K_H) a Siegel triple for H with S_H ℚ-split (the general case reduces to this by conjugating with an element of R_u(P_H)(ℝ), Orr §4.1); K_G ⊂ G(ℝ) maximal compact with K_H ⊂ K_G whose Cartan involution stabilises S_H
proofSteps: Choose an order of the finite restricted roots extending the positive roots of H; RG2.1 constructs the parabolic Q and its centralizer Levi.
Cartan stability of S_H implies stability of Z_G(S_H), so K_G∩Z_G(S_H) is maximal compact there.
Uniqueness of the Cartan-stable Siegel torus gives S_H⊂S_G. Project to P_G/N_G; maximal splitness in P_H/N_H gives equality S_G∩H=S_H.
acceptance: G = SL_2, K_G = SO(2), H = S_H = P_H the diagonal torus, K_H = {±1}: Z_G(S_H) = H, Q = P_G is a Borel containing H, S_G = H and S_G ∩ H = H. For the Orr–Schnell §B torus H = {(x, x⁻¹−x; 0, x⁻¹)}, g ↦ (gᵀ)⁻¹ does not stabilise S_H = H, so the hypothesis fails (and the containment theorem fails there).

sources.match: Construction of Q and P_G and the torus comparisons, with S_H taken ℚ-split (reduction in §4.1); Lemma 4.4 needs the Cartan-stability hypothesis added by Orr–Schnell §A.
The corrected Cartan-stability and zero-weight hypotheses are imposed.

nodes.title: Finite root-cone comparison
nodes.statement: In containment-parabolic-torus, for any t>0 there is t′∈(0,1] such that every a∈A_{H,t} belongs to wA_{G,t′}w⁻¹ for some w in the finite Weyl group of S_G satisfying N_H,N_Z⊂wN_Gw⁻¹. Roots of S_G vanishing on S_H take the value 1 ≥ t′ on a, so they impose no further condition.
hypotheses: the notation and hypotheses of containment-parabolic-torus (S_H ℚ-split, K_H ⊂ K_G, Cartan involution of K_G stabilising S_H); Z = Z_G(S_H), N_Z = R_u(P_G ∩ Z); t > 0
proofSteps: Choose a maximal root subset Ψ with nonnegative logarithmic values at a whose union with the positive H-roots admits an order.
Maximality makes every root positive for this order a nonnegative linear combination of the H-simple roots and Ψ. Finitely many subsets give a uniform bound on coefficient sums, hence t′.

Form the corresponding parabolic and use Weyl conjugacy of minimal parabolics; its unipotent radical contains both N_H and N_Z. Roots restricting to zero have value one, as required by the correction.
acceptance: G = SL_2, K_G = SO(2), H = S_H the diagonal torus: Δ_H = ∅, so A_{H,t} = {diag(s, s⁻¹) : s > 0}; with t′ = 1, w = 1 serves s ≥ 1 and the nontrivial Weyl element serves s ≤ 1, and no single w serves every a.

sources.match: The finite cone bound through a maximal root subset and a uniform coefficient bound; the zero-restriction case is the Orr–Schnell §E correction.
The corrected Cartan-stability and zero-weight hypotheses are imposed.

nodes.title: Rational and compact Weyl representatives
nodes.statement: For each admissible Weyl element w in containment-finite-root-cones, choose a compact representative w_K∈K_G and a representative w_Q=u⁻¹w′_Qu with w′_Q∈G(ℚ), u∈N_Z(ℝ), and w′_Q⁻¹w_Q∈N_G(ℝ). Their quotient can be chosen in the identity component of Z_G(S_G)(ℝ).
hypotheses: the notation and hypotheses of containment-finite-root-cones; w ranges over the finite set of Weyl elements of S_G with N_H, N_Z ⊂ wN_Gw⁻¹; u ∈ N_Z(ℝ) with uS_Gu⁻¹ a maximal ℚ-split torus of P_G ∩ Z; the maximal real split torus containing S_G is chosen stable under the Cartan involution of K_G
proofSteps: Conjugate S_G by u to a rational maximal split torus; use rational relative-Weyl representatives requested from RG2.1.
Choose a Cartan-stable maximal real split torus containing S_G. Real Weyl representatives lie in K_G by the LieGroups contract.
Admissibility implies u and w_Q⁻¹u⁻¹w_Q lie in N_G; their product is w′_Q⁻¹w_Q. Adjust the compact representative by the centralizer compact subgroup to match components.
acceptance: G = SL_2, K_G = SO(2), H the diagonal torus: u = 1, and for the nontrivial Weyl element w_K = w_Q = w′_Q = (0, −1; 1, 0), which lies in SL_2(ℚ) ∩ SO(2), so w′_Q⁻¹w_Q = 1 ∈ N_G(ℝ).

sources.match: Rational representatives through the unipotent conjugation, compact representatives in K_G, and the unipotent quotient for admissible Weyl elements; the original lemma does not require the real split torus to be Cartan-stable, which is the Orr–Schnell §E correction.
The corrected Cartan-stability and zero-weight hypotheses are imposed.

nodes.title: Uniform compact factors for subgroup Siegel sets
nodes.statement: With Ω_H⊂N_HM_H compact, choose a compact Ω_G⊂N_GM_G and, for every admissible w, a compact B_w⊂S_G(ℝ)^0 such that w′_Q⁻¹Ω_H⊂Ω_G w_K⁻¹ B_w K_Z. All these choices range over a finite Weyl set.
hypotheses: the notation and hypotheses of containment-weyl-representatives; Ω_H ⊂ N_H(ℝ)M_H(ℝ)^+ compact; K_Z = K_G ∩ Z_G(S_H)(ℝ), maximal compact in Z_G(S_H)(ℝ) by the Cartan hypothesis
proofSteps: Use the unipotent/Levi product homeomorphism to factor Ω_H into compact subsets of N_H and M_H.
Apply Iwasawa in Z_G(S_H) to the latter compact set; then Langlands coordinates in its minimal parabolic give compact N_Z,M_G,S_G factors.
Conjugate by the representatives from containment-weyl-representatives. The unipotent inclusion and normalization of M_G put the finite union in N_GM_G.
acceptance: G = SL_2, K_G = SO(2), H the diagonal torus: M_H(ℝ)^+ = 1 and N_H = 1, so Ω_H ⊂ {1}; with w_K = w′_Q for both admissible w, Ω_G = {1}, B_w = {1} and K_Z = {±1} satisfy w′_Q⁻¹Ω_H ⊂ Ω_G w_K⁻¹ B_w K_Z.

sources.match: Compact coordinates are assembled once over the finite set.
The corrected Cartan-stability and zero-weight hypotheses are imposed.

nodes.title: Finite covolume of a projection closure
nodes.statement: Let Γ be a lattice in locally compact second-countable groups A×B, and Δ the closure of its B-projection. Then Δ\B carries a nonzero finite B-invariant Radon measure.
hypotheses: A and B second countable locally compact Hausdorff groups; Γ ⊂ A×B a lattice: a discrete subgroup with a nonzero finite (A×B)-invariant Radon measure on Γ\(A×B); B acts on Γ\(A×B) and on Δ\B by right translation in the second factor
proofSteps: The map Γ\(A×B)→Δ\B induced by projection is continuous, surjective and B-equivariant.
Push forward the normalized finite invariant measure on the lattice quotient.
Finite regularity on the countably generated locally compact quotient gives a Radon probability measure; invariance and nonzeroness are preserved.
acceptance: Γ = {(x, σx) : x ∈ ℤ[√2]} is a lattice in ℝ×ℝ with dense second projection, so Δ = ℝ and Δ\B is a point of mass 1. Dropping the lattice hypothesis fails: Γ = ℤ×{0} is discrete in ℝ×ℝ, Δ = {0} and Δ\B = ℝ has no nonzero finite invariant measure.

sources.match: The finite-covolume projection step is separated from openness.

nodes.title: Native-field Lie algebra of an arithmetic closure
nodes.statement: For absolutely almost simple G/F, S containing all infinite places with G(F_S) noncompact, and finite nonempty S₁ disjoint from S, the closure of G(O_{F,S∪S₁}) in ∏_{v∈S₁}G(F_v) has full native F_v Lie algebra in every factor and, for the places of S₁ above one rational prime p, no proper graph Lie subalgebra of the ℚ_p-Lie algebra of ∏_{v|p}G(F_v) linking distinct places (places above distinct primes are separated by the pro-p splitting of compact open subgroups). This is an arithmetic statement requiring the full S-integral subgroup, rather than mere F_v-Zariski density.
hypotheses: F a number field; G connected absolutely almost simple over F; S a finite set of places containing all archimedean places with G_S noncompact; S₁ a finite nonempty set of finite places disjoint from S
proofSteps: The projection-finite-covolume and S-arithmetic nondiscreteness inputs provide a positive-dimensional closed analytic subgroup.
For ℚ with one additional isotropic prime use Rapinchuk §2.6 and the ℚ_p closed-subgroup argument.

For general F and multiple places the restriction-of-scalars trace-field and independent-factor argument is a recorded input. Without it SL₂(ℚ_p) inside SL₂(E) is a counterexample to native-E openness.
acceptance: F = ℚ(i), G = SL_2, S = {∞}, S₁ = the two places above 5 = (2+i)(2−i), so ∏_{v∈S₁}G(F_v) = SL_2(ℚ_5)²: the closure of the full group SL_2(ℤ[i][1/5]) has ℚ_5-Lie algebra sl_2(ℚ_5)² of dimension 6, whereas the subgroup SL_2(ℤ[1/5]) has closure the diagonal, a graph subgroup with 3-dimensional Lie algebra, so Zariski density of a subgroup alone does not suffice.

sources.locator: §§2.6–2.7, proof of Theorem 2.3 and reference to Platonov–Rapinchuk §7.4
sources.match: The surveyed proof treats the single-prime ℚ branch; the general arithmetic input remains explicit.

nodes.title: Openness in a finite product of completions
nodes.statement: Given arithmetic-native-lie-closure and Cartan's closed-subgroup theorem (recorded gap) applied, for each rational prime p, to the ℚ_p-analytic group ∏_{v∈S₁, v|p}G(F_v), the closure Δ of G(O_{F,S∪S₁}) is open in that finite product. Its index is finite by projection-finite-covolume.
hypotheses: F a number field; G connected absolutely almost simple over F; S a finite set of places containing the archimedean places with G_S noncompact; S₁ a finite nonempty set of finite places disjoint from S
proofSteps: A closed analytic subgroup with the full product Lie algebra has the same dimension and contains an identity neighbourhood by the inverse function theorem.
Apply open-finite-covolume-finite-index to the nonzero finite invariant quotient measure. Full projections alone would not exclude graph subgroups.

Places above distinct primes: a compact open subgroup of ∏_{v∈S₁}G(F_v) contains ∏_p P_p with P_p an open pro-p subgroup of ∏_{v|p}G(F_v); a closed subgroup of ∏_p P_p is pronilpotent, hence the product of its Sylow subgroups C_p ⊂ P_p, so openness of Δ is checked one prime at a time.
acceptance: G = SL_2 over ℚ, S = {∞}, S₁ = {2, 3}: the closure of SL_2(ℤ[1/6]) in SL_2(ℚ_2) × SL_2(ℚ_3) is open (in fact everything). Full projections do not suffice: over F = ℚ(i) with S₁ the two places above 5, the diagonal closure of SL_2(ℤ[1/5]) in SL_2(ℚ_5)² is closed with both projections onto SL_2(ℚ_5) but is not open.

sources.match: The product Lie hypothesis is essential.

nodes.title: Elimination of arithmetic finite-index closures
nodes.statement: For G/F absolutely almost simple simply connected, S containing infinity with G(F_S) noncompact, and S₁ finite disjoint from S, an open finite-index closure of G(O_{F,S∪S₁}) in ∏_{v∈S₁}G(F_v) is the whole product. At isotropic factors this follows from the local Kneser–Tits/Tits finite-index theorem; anisotropic factors need the separate global arithmetic congruence argument.
hypotheses: F a number field; G connected, absolutely almost simple and simply connected over F; S a finite set of places containing the archimedean places with G_S noncompact; S₁ a finite set of finite places disjoint from S; the closure of G(𝒪_{F,S∪S₁}) in G_{S₁} is open of finite index
proofSteps: Take the finite normal core of the closure.
At every isotropic factor the precise RG2.4 finite-index theorem makes that factor trivial in the finite quotient.

For anisotropic compact factors the finite quotient can be nontrivial for an arbitrary open subgroup. Eliminating it for this arithmetic subgroup is a distinct recorded global input; weak approximation does not impose integrality away from S∪S₁.
acceptance: Simple connectedness is needed: for PGL_2 over ℚ, S = {∞}, S₁ = {5}, determinants of PGL_2(ℤ[1/5]) are ±5^k, which lie in {1, 5}·ℚ_5^{×2} since −1 is a square in ℚ_5, so the closure is a proper open subgroup of index 2 in PGL_2(ℚ_5). At an anisotropic factor an arbitrary open subgroup can be proper of finite index: for B ramified exactly at 2 and 3, SL_1(B ⊗ ℚ_2) has proper principal congruence subgroups.

sources.match: The isotropic proof does not silently cover compact anisotropic factors.

nodes.title: Eigenvalues of algebraic tensor subquotients
nodes.statement: For a closed faithful algebraic representation ρ of a finite-type affine group G over a characteristic-zero field and any algebraic representation σ, every eigenvalue of σ(g) over an algebraic closure lies in the multiplicative subgroup generated by the eigenvalues of ρ(g).
hypotheses: k a field of characteristic 0 with algebraic closure k̄; G an affine group scheme of finite type over k; ρ : G → GL(V) a closed immersion; σ : G → GL(W) an algebraic representation; g ∈ G(k)
proofSteps: Request the algebraic comodule theorem that σ is a subquotient of a finite direct sum of tensor words in ρ and ρ∨.
Triangularize the action of g over the algebraic closure. Tensor eigenvalues are products and dual eigenvalues are inverses.
Invariant subspaces and quotient spaces take subsets of the triangular diagonal eigenvalues.
acceptance: G = G_m over ℚ, ρ = the identity character, σ = t⁻² ⊕ t³: for g = 2 the eigenvalues 1/4 and 8 lie in ⟨2⟩. Algebraicity is needed: the injective abstract homomorphism ℚ^× → ℂ^×, a ↦ sign(a)|a|^{√2}, sends 2 to 2^{√2}, and the eigenvalue 2 of the algebraic σ = t is not in ⟨2^{√2}⟩.

sources.match: Neatness for one faithful representation implies it for every representation over a subfield of ℂ, because every representation is built from one faithful representation.

nodes.title: Stable lattices for compact p-adic matrix groups
nodes.statement: Every compact subgroup C⊂GL_n(ℚ_p) preserves a full ℤ_p-lattice Λ⊂ℚ_p^n. It is conjugate into GL_n(ℤ_p).
hypotheses: p a prime; n ≥ 1; C ⊂ GL_n(ℚ_p) a compact subgroup
proofSteps: Compactness bounds all entries of C, so Cℤ_p^n lies in p^−Mℤ_p^n for one M.
Let Λ be the ℤ_p-span of Cℤ_p^n. It contains ℤ_p^n, is contained in p^−Mℤ_p^n, and is C-stable.
Noetherianity and the PID property give a free rank-n lattice; choose its basis.
acceptance: C = {1, s} with s = (0 p; p⁻¹ 0) (s² = 1) is not in GL_2(ℤ_p) but preserves Λ = ℤ_p ⊕ p⁻¹ℤ_p, and h = diag(1, p⁻¹) gives h⁻¹sh = (0 1; 1 0) ∈ GL_2(ℤ_p). Compactness is needed: ⟨diag(p, 1)⟩ is unbounded and preserves no lattice.

sources.match: Arithmetic subgroups contain neat finite-index subgroups cut out by congruence conditions modulo N; the source refers the proof to Borel 17.4, so this p-adic input is supplied here rather than read in the source.

nodes.title: Distance of p-adic roots of unity from one
nodes.statement: If ζ≠1 is a root of unity in an algebraic closure of ℚ_p, then |ζ−1|_p≥p^{−1/(p−1)}. More precisely a primitive p^k-th root has distance p^{−1/(p^{k−1}(p−1))}, while a root of order prime to p has distance one.
hypotheses: p a prime; ℚ̄_p an algebraic closure of ℚ_p with the unique extension of |·|_p; ζ ∈ ℚ̄_p a root of unity
proofSteps: Reduction on prime-to-p roots of unity is injective: Hensel uniqueness for T^m−1 and its unit derivative gives distance one for a nontrivial such root.
For a primitive p^k-root, evaluate the cyclotomic polynomial at one to obtain p=∏(1−ζ^a), over a prime to p.
The conjugates have the same extended p-adic absolute value, so each factor has absolute value p^−1/φ(p^k). Combine the prime-to-p and p-primary parts.
acceptance: |ζ_3 − 1|_3 = 3^{−1/2} (the norm of 1 − ζ_3 is Φ_3(1) = 3), attaining the bound for p = 3; over ℚ_2, |i − 1|_2 = 2^{−1/2} and |−1 − 1|_2 = 2^{−1} = 2^{−1/(2−1)}, so −1 lies on the boundary of the excluded ball; a primitive 6th root of unity has |ζ_6 − 1|_2 = 1.

sources.match: Arithmetic subgroups contain neat finite-index subgroups cut out by congruence conditions modulo N; the source refers the proof to Borel 17.4, so this p-adic input is supplied here rather than read in the source.

nodes.title: Eigenvalue bound for congruence matrices
nodes.statement: If M∈1+p^a M_n(ℤ_p), every eigenvalue λ of M in ℚ̄_p satisfies |λ−1|_p≤p^−a. The eigenvalues and their inverses then lie in the multiplicative open ball used by padic-ball-torsion-free when p≥3,a≥1 or p=2,a≥2.
hypotheses: p a prime; a ≥ 1; M ∈ 1 + p^a M_n(ℤ_p); eigenvalues taken in ℚ̄_p with the extended absolute value
proofSteps: An eigenvalue μ of an integral matrix has |μ|_p≤1, by its monic integral characteristic polynomial.
Apply this to (M−1)/p^a; λ=1+p^aμ.
Ultrametric multiplication and inversion preserve the ball about one.
acceptance: M = (1 3; 3 1) ∈ 1 + 3M_2(ℤ_3) has eigenvalues 4 and −2 with |4 − 1|_3 = |−2 − 1|_3 = 1/3. At p = 2 the level a ≥ 2 is needed for the ball: M = −1 ∈ 1 + 2M_1(ℤ_2) has eigenvalue −1 with |−1 − 1|_2 = 1/2, not < 2^{−1}.

sources.match: Arithmetic subgroups contain neat finite-index subgroups cut out by congruence conditions modulo N; the source refers the proof to Borel 17.4, so this p-adic input is supplied here rather than read in the source.

nodes.title: Compact kernel of height on an archimedean level
nodes.statement: For connected reductive G/F let K∞⊂G(F∞) be closed, contain A_G(ℝ)^0, and be compact modulo it. Then K∞∩ker H_{G,∞} is compact, and multiplication gives K∞≃A_G(ℝ)^0×(K∞∩ker H_{G,∞}).
hypotheses: F a number field; G connected reductive over F with A_G the maximal ℚ-split central torus of Res_{F/ℚ}G; K∞ ⊂ G(F_∞) a closed subgroup containing A_G(ℝ)^0 with K∞/A_G(ℝ)^0 compact; H_{G,∞} : G(F_∞) → 𝔞_G the archimedean log-height of AA.2
proofSteps: The archimedean height restricts to a topological isomorphism on A_G(ℝ)^0.
Map k to (a(H∞(k)),a(H∞(k))⁻¹k); centrality makes this a group and topological product decomposition.
Its kernel factor is homeomorphic to K∞/A_G(ℝ)^0, hence compact.
acceptance: GL_2/ℚ with K∞ = ℝ^×O(2): A_G(ℝ)^0 = ℝ_{>0}, H_{G,∞} = log|det|, and K∞ ∩ ker H_{G,∞} = O(2) is compact. Dropping compactness modulo A_G fails: for K∞ = GL_2(ℝ) the kernel {|det| = 1} is noncompact.

sources.match: The compact kernel removes the noncompact split-centre direction.

nodes.title: Finite full rational stabilizers
nodes.statement: Under compact-kernel-split-centre and for compact open U⊂G(𝔸_f), A_x=G(F)∩gK∞Ug⁻¹ is finite. Here A_x is the full stabilizer, before division by any rational central subgroup.
hypotheses: F a number field; G connected reductive over F; K∞ ⊂ G(F_∞) closed, containing A_G(ℝ)^0 and compact modulo it; U ⊂ G(𝔸_{F,f}) compact open; g ∈ G(𝔸_F)
proofSteps: Every rational character has total adelic norm one on a rational point by the product formula.
Its finite component lies in g_fUg_f⁻¹, a compact group; every positive-real character norm is one there. Its archimedean height is therefore zero.
Conjugate the archimedean point into the compact kernel of K∞. The full adelic stabilizer lies in a compact product, whose intersection with the closed discrete rational subgroup is finite.
acceptance: GL_2/ℚ, K∞ = ℝ^×SO(2), U = GL_2(ℤ̂), g = 1: A_x = GL_2(ℤ) ∩ ℝ^×SO(2) = {±1, ±S} with S = (0 −1; 1 0), of order 4 (positive determinant forces det 1 and then the scalar is ±1). Dropping the hypothesis on K∞ fails: for F = ℚ(√2), G = G_m, K∞ = (F ⊗ ℝ)^× and U = Ô_F^×, A_x = 𝒪_F^× is infinite.

sources.match: The proof uses the full product formula, not an arbitrary noncompact K∞.

nodes.title: Proper arithmetic action on the level space
nodes.statement: Under rational-stabilizer-finite, the discrete group G(F) acts properly discontinuously on G(𝔸)/K∞U with its canonical quotient topology: for compact C,D only finitely many γ satisfy γC∩D≠∅.
hypotheses: F a number field; G connected reductive over F; K∞ ⊂ G(F_∞) closed, containing A_G(ℝ)^0 and compact modulo it; U ⊂ G(𝔸_{F,f}) compact open; G(F) acts on G(𝔸)/K∞U by left multiplication
proofSteps: Use the split-centre quotient homeomorphism G(𝔸)/A_G(ℝ)^0≃G(𝔸)^1. The residual right subgroup is compact by compact-kernel-split-centre and compactness of U.
The quotient by this compact subgroup has compact lifts for compact subsets, using finite covers by relatively compact quotient neighbourhoods.
If γC∩D is nonempty, γ lies in the compact product of the lifts and the compact right subgroup. The rational subgroup is closed discrete, so only finitely many such γ occur.
acceptance: GL_2/ℚ, K∞ = ℝ^×SO(2), U = GL_2(ℤ̂), C = D = {the base coset}: the γ ∈ GL_2(ℚ) with γC ∩ D ≠ ∅ form GL_2(ℤ) ∩ ℝ^×SO(2) = {±1, ±S}, four elements. Dropping the hypothesis on K∞ fails: for F = ℚ(√2), G = G_m, K∞ = (F ⊗ ℝ)^×, U = Ô_F^×, every point of G(𝔸)/K∞U ≅ 𝔸_f^×/Ô_F^× has the infinite stabilizer 𝒪_F^×.

sources.match: Canonical quotient topology and compact lifts precede the covering theorem.

nodes.title: Fibre mass for full stabilizers
nodes.statement: Let U′⊂U be compact open and let A_x=G(F)∩gK∞Ug⁻¹ be finite. For the full stabilizers A_y at the points above x, ∑_{y↦x}1/|A_y|=[U:U′]/|A_x|.
hypotheses: F a number field; G connected reductive over F; K∞ ⊂ G(F_∞) closed; U′ ⊂ U ⊂ G(𝔸_{F,f}) compact open; x = [g] ∈ X_U with A_x = G(F) ∩ gK∞Ug⁻¹ finite (for example by rational-stabilizer-finite)
proofSteps: The finite group A_x acts on U/U′ through the finite component of g⁻¹A_xg.
The fibre is its orbit set and each orbit stabilizer is the corresponding full A_y.
For each orbit |orbit|=|A_x|/|A_y|. Sum these equalities over the finite coset set.
acceptance: SL_2/ℚ, K∞ = SO(2), U = SL_2(ℤ̂), U′ = U ∩ K_0(2), x = [i]: A_x = {±1, ±S} has order 4 and [U:U′] = 3. The fibre has the elliptic point of Γ_0(2) (A_y of order 4, generated by (1 −1; 2 −1)) and one further point with A_y = {±1}, so 1/4 + 1/2 = 3/4 = [U:U′]/|A_x|.

sources.match: Discrete subgroups meet compact sets in finitely many elements (the kernel sum is finite); the orbit–stabilizer count itself is elementary and not in the source.

nodes.title: Integral lifting for reductive abelianization
nodes.statement: For connected reductive G/F with simply connected derived group and ν:G→D=G/G^der, there is a finite set B such that smooth reductive models over O_{F,B} extend ν and ν:G(O_v)→D(O_v) is surjective for every finite v∉B.
hypotheses: F a number field; G connected reductive over F with G^der simply connected; D = G/G^der and ν : G → D the quotient morphism
proofSteps: Spread the quotient and its simply connected derived kernel to smooth models with geometrically connected fibres, as requested from RG2.3.
A fibre over d∈D(O_v) is a smooth torsor under the connected derived model. Lang vanishing over the finite residue field supplies a residue point.
Hensel lifting supplies an O_v-point of that fibre, which is the required integral lift.
acceptance: GL_n with ν = det: B can be empty, and det(diag(u, 1, …, 1)) = u lifts every u ∈ ℤ_p^×. Connected kernel fibres are needed: t ↦ t² on G_m has kernel μ_2, and ℤ_p^× → ℤ_p^× misses the nonsquare units for every odd p.

sources.match: For almost all primes the map from integral points of G to integral points of its abelianization is surjective: spread out to a smooth morphism with connected kernel fibres, use Lang's lemma over the residue field and lift by Hensel.

nodes.title: Surjectivity of finite adelic abelianization
nodes.statement: Under abelianization-integral-lifts and local simply connected H¹ vanishing, ν:G(𝔸_f)→D(𝔸_f) is surjective with kernel G^der(𝔸_f). It is the actual restricted-product homomorphism induced by ν.
hypotheses: F a number field; G connected reductive over F with G^der simply connected; D = G/G^der and ν : G → D the quotient morphism with its restricted-product map on finite adelic points
proofSteps: At each exceptional finite place use the torsor fibre and kneser-local-torsor to lift the local point.
At almost all places lift the integral point integrally by abelianization-integral-lifts.
These lifts assemble into a restricted-product element. The kernel is identified placewise with the derived group, with the same integral compatibility.
acceptance: GL_n/F with ν = det: t ↦ diag(t, 1, …, 1) is a section 𝔸_{F,f}^× → GL_n(𝔸_{F,f}), integral wherever t is, and the kernel is SL_n(𝔸_{F,f}). For G = B^× with B a definite quaternion algebra over ℚ ramified at p, Nrd : G(𝔸_f) → 𝔸_f^× is surjective (every element of ℚ_p^× is a reduced norm at the ramified p), although Nrd(B^×) = ℚ_{>0} ≠ ℚ^×.

sources.match: With simply connected derived group the abelianization map on finite adelic points is surjective and maps compact open subgroups to compact open subgroups: local surjectivity at every prime from vanishing local H¹ of the derived group, plus integral surjectivity at almost all primes.

nodes.title: Integral compatibility of a central derived cover
nodes.statement: For the actual simply connected central cover ρ:G̃→G^der, at almost every finite place v one has ρ(G̃(F_v))∩G^der(O_v)=ρ(G̃(O_v)). Consequently the adelic image is exactly the restricted product of the local images with these integral image subgroups.
hypotheses: F a number field; G connected reductive over F; ρ : G̃ → G^der the simply connected central cover of the derived group (a central isogeny), extended with G̃, G^der to smooth affine models over 𝒪_{F,B} for a finite set B (RG2.3 request)
proofSteps: Extend ρ as a finite morphism of integral models away from finitely many places.
A local lift over F_v of an integral target point extends over O_v by the valuative criterion for properness of a finite morphism.
Choose such integral lifts almost everywhere and assemble them adelically.
acceptance: ρ : SL_2 → PGL_2 over ℚ, p odd: ρ(SL_2(ℚ_p)) = {g : det g ∈ ℚ_p^{×2}} has index 4 in PGL_2(ℚ_p); its intersection with PGL_2(ℤ_p) = GL_2(ℤ_p)/ℤ_p^× is {det ∈ ℤ_p^{×2}}, of index 2, and equals ρ(SL_2(ℤ_p)) since g with det g = u² gives u⁻¹g ∈ SL_2(ℤ_p).

sources.locator: §2.3, arXiv v3 p. 15 (definition of G(R)^+); used in Definition 3.1, p. 22
sources.match: The actual algebraic cover, rather than an arbitrary point homomorphism, defines the plus subgroup.

nodes.title: Compact idele classes modulo squares
nodes.statement: Let C_F=F×\𝔸_F× be the idele class group of a number field. Then C_F/C_F² is compact Hausdorff: the norm decomposition C_F≃ℝ_{>0}×C_F¹ identifies it with the quotient of compact C_F¹ by its square image.
hypotheses: F a number field; C_F = F^×\𝔸_F^× with the quotient topology and C_F² its subgroup of squares; the idele norm and the compactness of C_F^1 from GlobalNumberFields layer 6
proofSteps: The norm-one idele class group is compact by the GlobalNumberFields layer-6 contract.
Squaring is surjective on ℝ_{>0}. The image of squaring on the compact norm-one factor is compact and hence closed.
The resulting quotient is compact Hausdorff. The local idele square-class group itself remains noncompact.
acceptance: For F = ℚ, 𝔸^× = ℚ^× × ℝ_{>0} × ℤ̂^× gives C_ℚ ≅ ℝ_{>0} × ℤ̂^× and C_ℚ/C_ℚ² ≅ ℤ̂^×/ℤ̂^{×2} = ∏_p ℤ_p^×/ℤ_p^{×2}, an infinite compact group of exponent 2. Before dividing by ℚ^× the analogue fails: 𝔸^×/𝔸^{×2} maps onto the infinite discrete ⊕_p ℤ/2 (valuations mod 2), so it is not compact.

sources.locator: Definition 3.1, arXiv v3 p. 22, and Remark 3.7, p. 25
sources.match: Compactness appears only after quotienting by rational points.

nodes.title: Fourier convergence of quadratic-character kernels
nodes.statement: Let C be a compact Hausdorff abelian group and χ_i:C→{±1} pairwise distinct nontrivial continuous characters. For each fixed character ψ of C, the Haar integral of ψ over ker χ_i is zero unless ψ=1 or ψ=χ_i, and hence these kernel Haar probabilities converge weakly to Haar probability on C.
hypotheses: C a compact Hausdorff abelian group; χ_i : C → {±1} pairwise distinct nontrivial continuous characters; m_i the Haar probability of the closed subgroup ker χ_i, viewed on C
proofSteps: A character restricted to a compact subgroup has integral zero unless trivial, by Haar translation invariance.
A character trivial on ker χ_i factors through C/ker χ_i≃{±1}, so it is 1 or χ_i.
For each fixed nontrivial ψ there is at most one exceptional i. Character separation and Stone–Weierstrass, supplied by CompactGroups layer 5, extend convergence to all continuous functions.
acceptance: C = (ℤ/2)^ℕ with χ_i(x) = (−1)^{x_i}: for ψ(x) = (−1)^{x_1+x_2} every ∫ψ dm_i is 0, and for ψ = χ_1 only m_1 gives 1, so ∫ψ dm_i → 0 = ∫ψ dHaar_C. Distinctness is needed: for χ_i = χ_1 constant, m_i = Haar(ker χ_1) has ∫χ_1 dm_i = 1 and does not tend to Haar_C.

sources.locator: Proposition 3.6, arXiv v3 p. 24, and its proof with Remark 3.7, p. 25
sources.match: Distinct quadratic characters give the Fourier limit without presuming a full Chabauty–Pontryagin theorem.

nodes.title: Limits of Haar measures on diagonal cosets
nodes.statement: For compact abelian C, closed H_i≤C with H_i→H through the quadratic-kernel setting, and points z_i∈C×C, every weak limit of Haar probabilities on z_iH_i^Δ is H^Δ-invariant and supported on one coset of H^Δ. The analogous statement holds when H_i=H is fixed.
hypotheses: C a compact Hausdorff abelian group; either H_i = ker χ_i for pairwise distinct quadratic characters χ_i : C → {±1} (then H = C) or H_i = H a fixed closed subgroup; z_i ∈ C × C; Haar probabilities on the cosets z_iH_i^Δ
proofSteps: For a character (ψ₁,ψ₂) of C×C, the integral along H_i^Δ is zero unless ψ₁ψ₂ is trivial on H_i.
The quadratic-kernel Fourier computation gives invariance under H^Δ for every weak limit.

The quotient by C^Δ is constant on each moving coset when H=C; its pushforward is a Dirac probability, and the Dirac image of a compact group is closed. For fixed H use the quotient by H^Δ instead. Thus the limit remains supported on one coset.
acceptance: C = (ℤ/2)^ℕ, H_i = ker(x ↦ (−1)^{x_i}), z_i = (0, e_1): every limit is Haar on {(c, c + e_1)}, which is C^Δ-invariant and one coset of C^Δ. Translations may move: with H fixed and z_i alternating between (0, 0) and (0, e_1), there are two limit points and no convergence.

sources.locator: Proposition 3.6, arXiv v3 p. 24, and Remark 3.7, p. 25
sources.match: The translations may move; only limit points are asserted.

nodes.title: Arithmetic closure at one isotropic place
nodes.statement: Let G be connected, absolutely almost simple and simply connected over a number field F, S a finite set of places containing the archimedean ones with G_S noncompact, v ∉ S a finite place at which G is F_v-isotropic, and W ⊂ G(𝔸_F^{S∪{v}}) a compact open subgroup. Then the image of Γ_W = G(F) ∩ (G_S × G(F_v) × W) is dense in G(F_v). Consequently the closure of G(F)G_S in G(𝔸_F) contains G(F_v), placed at v.
hypotheses: F a number field; G connected, absolutely almost simple and simply connected over F
S finite, containing the archimedean places, with G_S noncompact
v ∉ S a finite place with G isotropic over F_v; W ⊂ G(𝔸_F^{S∪{v}}) a compact open subgroup
proofSteps: Γ_W is a lattice in G_S × G(F_v) (AA.3/s-arithmetic-lattice for S ∪ {v}) and its image in G(F_v) is not discrete (s-arithmetic-nondiscrete with S₁ = {v}).

The closure Δ of that image carries a nonzero finite invariant quotient measure (projection-finite-covolume) and is open in G(F_v) (arithmetic-native-lie-closure with S₁ = {v}, applied to the commensurable group Γ_W; with a single place no graph subalgebra can occur).

Δ has finite index (open-finite-covolume-finite-index), hence Δ = G(F_v) because G(F_v) has no proper subgroup of finite index for G simply connected, absolutely almost simple and F_v-isotropic (RG2.4 Kneser–Tits request).
For g ∈ G(F_v), an open V ∋ 1 in G(F_v) and W as above pick γ ∈ Γ_W with γ_v ∈ gV; then γ·(γ_S)⁻¹ ∈ G(F)G_S lies in {1} × gV × W. Shrinking V and W puts g, placed at v, in the closure of G(F)G_S.
acceptance: SL_2 over ℚ, S = {∞}, v = p, W = ∏_{q≠p} SL_2(ℤ_q): Γ_W = SL_2(ℤ[1/p]) is dense in SL_2(ℚ_p).

For G = SL_1(B), B the quaternion algebra over ℚ ramified exactly at 2 and 3 (so split at ∞ and G_∞ ≅ SL_2(ℝ) noncompact), the lemma applies at every p ≥ 5 but not at p = 2, 3, where G(ℚ_p) is compact and anisotropic; there density comes from weak approximation in strong-approximation-sufficiency.

sources.match: For ℚ and one isotropic prime the source argues: lattice, nondiscrete p-adic projection whose closure has finite covolume, Borel density, openness by the Lie-algebra argument, finite index, and equality since a simply connected isotropic group has no finite-index subgroups.
Simple connectedness enters only through the absence of proper finite-index subgroups of G(K_v) at the places outside S where G is isotropic.

nodes.title: Almost all local factors are isotropic
nodes.statement: Let G be a connected semisimple group of positive dimension over a number field F. Then G is quasi-split, hence isotropic, over F_v for all but finitely many places v. In particular, for finite S the set of places v ∉ S at which G is F_v-anisotropic is finite.
hypotheses: F a number field; G connected semisimple over F with dim G > 0
proofSteps: Outside a finite set of places G extends to a reductive group scheme over 𝒪_v that has a Borel 𝒪_v-subgroup (RG2.3 request: smooth reductive models and smoothness of their scheme of Borel subgroups; the Borel exists by Lang's theorem over the finite residue field, Tau Ceti ReductiveGroups layer 9 request, and Hensel lifting on the smooth scheme of Borel subgroups).
Its generic fibre is a Borel subgroup of G over F_v, a proper parabolic because G is not a torus, so G is F_v-isotropic (RG2.1 Borel–Tits criterion).
acceptance: For SL_1(B), B the quaternion algebra over ℚ ramified exactly at 2 and 3, the anisotropic places are exactly 2 and 3; SL_n over any F has none.

sources.match: Outside a finite set of places a connected reductive group over a number field is unramified, in particular quasisplit over the completion.

nodes.title: Canonical logarithmic torus at GL₁ level
nodes.statement: For the level U_Q of gl1-XQ-components, the identity component is the logarithmic quotient W/Λ_Q, where W=ℝ^{r₁+r₂}/ℝ·(1,…,1) and Λ_Q is the image of totally positive congruence units F×∩U_{Q,f}. It is a compact real torus of dimension r₁+r₂−1. The complex circle factors have already been divided out by K∞.
hypotheses: F a number field with r₁ real and r₂ complex places; Q a finite set of finite places, p a prime and n ≥ 1 with N(v) ≡ 1 mod p^n for v ∈ Q; U_Q = K_∞ × ∏_v U_{Q,v}, K_∞ and A_∞^0 as in gl1-XQ-components
proofSteps: Take absolute values and logarithms after quotienting the complex compact circles; positive real archimedean factors become ℝ^{r₁+r₂}.
The diagonal positive split centre becomes the constant line. Its quotient identifies with the product-formula weighted trace-zero hyperplane.
gl1-units-lattice gives a full lattice Λ_Q; a lattice basis identifies W/Λ_Q with a product of r₁+r₂−1 circles.
acceptance: F = ℚ(√2), Q = ∅: 1+√2 has norm −1, so it is not totally positive and moves the identity component to another component; Λ is generated by 3+2√2 = (1+√2)², and in the coordinate s = u₁ − u₂ on W the identity component is ℝ/(2 log(3+2√2))ℤ = ℝ/(4 log(1+√2))ℤ, not the circle ℝ/(2 log(1+√2))ℤ that all units would give. For F imaginary quadratic the identity component is a point.

sources.match: The level and component group are retained; the circle quotient precedes the dimension calculation.

nodes.title: GL₂ components for O(2) and SO(2)
nodes.statement: For GL₂/ℚ and principal finite level K(N), the quotient with K∞=ℝ×SO(2) has components (ℤ/N)× and raw real symmetric space ℍ± before rational orientation reduction. With K∞=ℝ×O(2), the real space is the folded ℍ and the component set is (ℤ/N)×/{±1}. At N=3 these cardinalities are respectively two and one.
hypotheses: G = GL₂ over ℚ; N ≥ 1 and K(N) = ker(GL₂(ℤ̂) → GL₂(ℤ/N)); K∞ = ℝ^×SO(2) with the raw Möbius action on ℍ±, or K∞ = ℝ^×O(2) with the folded action on ℍ
proofSteps: The positive determinant arithmetic subgroup gives the SO(2) component quotient ℚ_{>0}\𝔸_f×/det K(N).
Passing to O(2) allows rational negative-determinant matrices; their determinant adds the sign subgroup {±1} to the finite unit quotient.
Use the raw/folded action bridge, and compute the two finite unit quotients at N=3.
acceptance: N = 3: (ℤ/3)^× = {1, 2}, so ℝ^×SO(2) gives two components, each Γ(3)\ℍ; since −1 ≡ 2 mod 3, (ℤ/3)^×/{±1} is one point, so ℝ^×O(2) gives one component, again Γ(3)\ℍ (a rational unit determinant ≡ 1 mod 3 is 1). N = 5: four and two components. N = 1, 2: one component in both conventions.

sources.match: The real compact and determinant sign convention determine the components.

nodes.title: Closedness of the central rational product
nodes.statement: Let G be connected reductive over F and X a closed subgroup of Z(𝔸_F). If XZ(F) is closed in Z(𝔸_F), then XG(F) is closed in G(𝔸_F).
hypotheses: F a number field; G connected reductive over F with centre Z and adjoint quotient G → G^ad of kernel Z (RG2.1); X ≤ Z(𝔸_F) a closed subgroup with XZ(F) closed in Z(𝔸_F)
proofSteps: Map to G^ad(𝔸_F). The image of G(F) is a subgroup of the closed discrete set G^ad(F), so it is itself closed discrete.

Over each point of this discrete image, XG(F) is a translate of XZ(F), a closed subset of the closed fibre Z(𝔸_F). The union is closed because the image is closed discrete: a neighbourhood of any point meets at most one such fibre.
acceptance: For G = GL_2 over ℚ and X = A_G(ℝ)^0 = ℝ_{>0} (scalars at ∞), XZ(ℚ) = ℝ_{>0}ℚ^× is the kernel of the continuous map 𝔸^× → ℚ^×ℝ_{>0}\𝔸^× ≅ ℤ̂^×, hence closed, so ℝ_{>0}GL_2(ℚ) is closed in GL_2(𝔸). The hypothesis cannot be dropped: XG(F) ∩ Z(𝔸_F) = XZ(F).

sources.match: The closed central quotient is needed for the automorphic Hilbert space; the adjoint-fibre proof makes its central-product hypothesis explicit.

requests.need: The topology on X(R) = Hom_{alg}(A, R) for an affine scheme of finite type and an arbitrary Hausdorff topological ring R (not only a local field): the weakest topology making all evaluation maps continuous (Conrad, Proposition 2.1), with functoriality in X and in continuous ring maps R → R′ (embeddings, open and closed embeddings, discreteness: Conrad, Example 2.2), compatibility with fibre products, closed immersions to closed embeddings, local compactness when R is locally compact, the topological-group axioms for Hopf algebras, and compactness and openness of 𝒳(𝒪_v) in X(F_v) for affine models over 𝒪_v (Conrad, Example 2.3 and Corollary 3.7). AA.1 evaluates it on 𝔸_F, 𝔸_{F,f}, F_v, 𝒪_v and F ⊗ ℝ. Supply the finite-type affine-group coordinate-comodule theorem: every finite-dimensional algebraic representation is a subquotient of finite sums of tensor words in a closed faithful representation and its dual. This is not true for arbitrary faithful point-group homomorphisms. For an affine finite-type group G over a nonarchimedean local field, supply that 1 ∈ G(F_v) has a neighbourhood basis of compact open subgroups (van Dantzig, or congruence kernels of a closed embedding into GL_n).

Weil restriction Res_{E/F} for affine finite-type schemes along a finite separable extension of number fields, with the identification of points Res_{E/F}(X)(R) ≅ X(E ⊗_F R) natural in the F-algebra R and compatible with group structures. Supply the point comparison as an equivalence of group-valued functors natural in every continuous value-algebra map, its compatibility with morphisms in G, identity and tower base change, and the tensor-product associator. The adelic comparison uses the canonical topological F-algebra isomorphism E⊗_F A_F→A_E, not an arbitrary equivalence of point sets.

The Cartan decomposition G(E) = K M(E) K for connected reductive G over a nonarchimedean local field E of characteristic 0, with K a special maximal compact subgroup containing representatives of the relative Weyl group, and M = Z_G(A) for a maximal E-split torus A; together with compactness of M(E)/A(E)-modulo-M(E)^1 used to see that M(E) = A(E)·M(E)^1 up to finite index. In addition to existence of local Iwasawa factorization, supply openness and the local P-K integration formula with left Haar density δ_P(m)^−1 dn dm dk (or the equivalent quasi-invariant quotient cocycle), including normalized integral factorization at good places. The Kneser–Tits theorem over nonarchimedean local fields of characteristic 0 (RT-AREA-automorphic-1/7): for G simply connected, absolutely almost simple and isotropic over E, define G(E)^+ as the subgroup generated by the E-points of the unipotent radicals of E-parabolics and prove Platonov's theorem G(E) = G(E)^+, Tits's simplicity of G(E)^+ modulo its centre (using the Tits system of the Iwahori–Bruhat decomposition), and the consequence that G(E) has no proper subgroup of finite index and no proper noncentral normal subgroup. This is the sub-stage RG2.4:kneser-tits proposed in RT-AREA-automorphic-1.fixes.md; AA.4 consumes only the finite-index consequence.
Local compactness of the finite adele ring FiniteAdeleRing (𝓞 K) K, and the placewise projections as continuous K-algebra maps 𝔸_{K,f} → K_v.
Local compactness of the adele ring and the continuity of the diagonal K → 𝔸_K.

The idele group 𝔸_K^× with Mathlib's units topology is locally compact and Hausdorff, and RestrictedProduct.unitsEquiv is a homeomorphism for the finite part; the idele norm ‖·‖ : 𝔸_K^× → ℝ_{>0} as a continuous homomorphism trivial on K^×; compactness of the norm-one idele class group; density of K in 𝔸_{K,f} (denseRange_algebraMap_finiteAdeleRing). Strong approximation for the additive group: denseRange_algebraMap_finiteAdeleRing (K dense in 𝔸_{K,f}). Compactness of the norm-one idele class group IdeleClassGroup.normOne and the description of the identity component of the idele class group, for the GL_1 validation.

The base-change comparison adeleBaseChangeEquiv : 𝔸_K ⊗_K L ≃A[𝔸_K] 𝔸_L for a finite extension L/K, as a continuous algebra equivalence with the module topology on the source, compatible with the diagonal embeddings and with the decomposition 𝔸_K ⊗_K L = ∏_v (K_v ⊗_K L).

For a real reductive Lie group G(ℝ) (also G(ℂ) viewed as a real group) with maximal compact K: the KAK decomposition G = K·closure(A⁺)·K with Weyl group representatives in K, and the Iwasawa decomposition G = K A N. For a real reductive group and the specified rational parabolic, give the open P-K factorization, its δ_P^−1 integration density, and Cartan-stable Levi coordinates; mere surjectivity does not provide integration. Supply the nested reductive-subgroup Cartan restriction and conjugacy theorem of Borel–Harish-Chandra §1.8, used in the finite-chain induction §1.9.

Functoriality of normalized absolute values under a finite extension E/F: |x|_w for x ∈ F_v equals |x|_v^{[E_w:F_v]}, with the local degrees in the exponents, and the product formula, used to compare the gauge-form measures of Res_{E/F} G with those of G.

The relative discriminant ideal relDiscr 𝒪_F 𝒪_E and the tower formula |d_E| = |d_F|^{[E:F]} · N(relDiscr), used for the discriminant factors of Tamagawa measures under restriction of scalars. Supply the scalar Jacobian product for an arbitrary F-basis β of E, using finite lattice indices and real determinants with complex measure 2dxdy: ∏j_{β,v}=|d_F|^{[E:F]/2}|d_E|⁻¹/². Do not assert this factor at every individual finite place; an integral local basis has j=1.

Field-generic Borel–Tits structure theory over a field of characteristic 0 (in particular a number field): existence and G(F)-conjugacy of minimal F-parabolic subgroups and of maximal F-split tori; the relative root system Φ(S_0, G) with positive roots from a minimal parabolic and simple roots Δ_0; the bijection between subsets of Δ_0 and standard parabolics; the relative Bruhat decomposition G(F) = ⊔_w P_0(F) w P_0(F); and the Borel–Tits criterion that a connected reductive group has a proper F-parabolic iff its derived group is F-isotropic iff G(F) contains a nontrivial unipotent element. RG2.1 states these for local fields E; AA.3 needs them over a number field. For reductive H⊂G in characteristic zero, supply affineness of H\G and local finite-dimensionality of its rational coordinate comodule. This is the closed-orbit realization input (Borel–Harish-Chandra §3.8), not adelic orbit finiteness. Supply the canonical decomposition of a semisimple simply connected F-group as a product of restrictions of scalars of absolutely almost simple simply connected groups, including the correspondence between the places above S. Supply the actual central simply connected derived cover and its lifted conjugation/commutator morphism. For finite-type smooth geometrically connected characteristic-zero affine groups, the geometric character group is finitely generated and torsion free via the torus quotient; for reductive groups restriction to the connected centre is an isogeny on character lattices. Also supply the adjoint quotient with kernel the scheme-theoretic centre and its natural local/adelic point maps. Supply also that the relative Weyl group N(A)/Z(A) of a maximal split torus A fixes exactly X_*((Z(G)∩A)^0)⊗ℚ inside X_*(A)⊗ℚ, over number fields and over local fields of characteristic 0 including ℝ. For the fixed-K containment nodes supply also: the parabolic G_Ψ attached to an order on the roots of a non-maximal ℚ-split torus, with Levi subgroup its centraliser (Borel–Tits 4.15, 3.12–3.13); simple transitivity of the relative Weyl group on the minimal parabolics containing a maximal split torus (5.9); and rational representatives of relative Weyl elements (5.3).

For connected reductive G over a number field, spread out to a smooth reductive model at almost all finite places and choose hyperspecial compact integral points. At each such place choose a maximal F_v-split torus containing the given global maximal F-split torus; the local split rank can be larger. Supply good-position compatibility with this local torus for Iwasawa. A maximal global split torus need not itself be maximal locally. Extend the reductive abelianization morphism with simply connected derived kernel to smooth models away from finitely many places; identify its fibres as torsors and supply Hensel lifting. Also extend the derived central cover as a finite morphism of the models. For a reductive group scheme over 𝒪_v its scheme of Borel subgroups is smooth and projective (SGA 3, Exposé XXII), so Borel subgroups of the special fibre lift. Supply also that at almost all finite places the smooth reductive model has a Borel 𝒪_v-subgroup, so that G is quasi-split, hence isotropic when G is not a torus, over F_v (Lang’s theorem over the residue field and Hensel lifting on the smooth scheme of Borel subgroups); AA.4/isotropic-almost-everywhere uses it.
Weak approximation for number fields (weakApproximation_denseRange, already in Tau Ceti) and its congruence/sign corollaries.

For a quadratic extension E/ℚ, the quadratic character χ_E of ℚ^×\𝔸^× with kernel ℚ^× N_{E/ℚ}(𝔸_E^×) (global reciprocity and the norm index [𝔸^× : ℚ^× N 𝔸_E^×] = 2), viewed as a character of ℚ^×\𝔸^×/𝔸^{×2}.

Hasse–Minkowski for quadratic forms over ℚ in five variables, used to show that a positive rational number is a reduced norm of a definite quaternion algebra over ℚ (the Hasse–Schilling–Maass theorem for quaternion algebras). Also supply local isotropy of every five-dimensional form over ℚ_p (u(ℚ_p)=4), and the real indefinite criterion; indefiniteness at infinity alone is not the local-global hypothesis.

Layer 10 Chebotarev Dirichlet density and its consequence: infinitely many unramified finite places with any prescribed conjugacy class in the Galois group of the specified finite splitting extension. Layer 11 coefficient summatory functions do not supply this statement.

The analytic identification of Γ(N)\ℍ (and Γ₀, Γ₁ quotients) with the corresponding level quotients, as an isomorphism of analytic spaces with the functorial action, used to identify the GL_2/ℚ adelic component with the upper half-plane quotient.

For a strongly continuous unitary Hilbert-space representation of a compact abelian group, the orthogonal character-isotypic summands have dense Hilbert direct sum, with projections ∫χ(z)⁻¹R(z)dz. The central-character use first twists by an extension of ω′; no untwisted action on X/X′ is asserted. Also supply character separation and Fourier uniqueness of probability measures on compact abelian groups. For compact Hausdorff abelian groups, supply character separation, density of finite character sums in continuous functions, Haar character orthogonality and uniqueness of measures from Fourier coefficients. These are the exact inputs used by the quadratic-kernel limit, without a separate full Chabauty duality theorem.

Supply the uniform finite-field reductive order formula in terms of Frobenius on the geometric character lattice and fundamental degrees, implying L_v(X,1)#G(k_v)q_v^{-dim G}=1+O(q_v^{-2}) for good reductive models. This is finite-group structure input, separate from the adelic convergence theorem. Supply Lang vanishing for torsors under connected reductive groups over finite residue fields, for the integral lifting argument.

Supply the cohomology exterior-power calculation for a finite product of circles with constant ℤ_p coefficients, its vanishing above the number of factors, and naturality under translations homotopic to the identity. Use the homology/product input already owned by Stage 5.

remaining: Obtain the GlobalNumberFields layers 4–6 local compactness and units-topology suppliers; implement the normalized and convergent restricted-measure constructions and their semantic box/rescaling tests. No undecomposed internal mathematical gap is retained in AA.0.

Obtain RG2.0 affine-points topology and coordinate-comodule language, RG2.0a natural Weil restriction, and GlobalNumberFields layer 8 continuous adelic scalar extension. Implement the integral-model, point/topology comparisons and examples with those canonical structures.

Finish nonarchimedean gauge integration/change of variables, positive Artin leading coefficients and induction at ramified places, and the requested finite reductive order estimate. Supply Borel sections, measurable associated-line completion and LCA character extension in the central-character construction; closedness of XG(F) is central-product-closed and the quotient topology is pinned Mathlib. The quotient-integration and corrected density arguments are now decomposed.

Supply the primitive squared-weight closed-orbit estimate, general Hermite–Minkowski/Siegel overlap and transfer to parabolic domains, Cholesky pivot and deep root-intersection estimates, geometry-of-numbers rational height counting, and the nonreductive/disconnected Levi extensions. Obtain RG2.1/RG2.3 and real/local Iwasawa integration suppliers.

Supply native-field arithmetic closure and exclusion of graph Lie subalgebras, anisotropic finite-index elimination, p-adic analytic closed-subgroup theory, Borel density, local/global simply connected cohomology and torus/central-cover obstruction proofs. Obtain integral-cover, Lang/Hensel and Kneser–Tits suppliers; finish quaternion norm topology. Implement neatness and quotient/Hecke maps using the actual algebraic representations and canonical topology.

Obtain the unit/logarithm/idele topology and torus cohomology suppliers; implement the SO(2)/O(2) comparisons for the specified levels. Supply the concrete Hurwitz class-number/unit enumeration and level-3 Eichler unit-index checks.

gaps.title: Measures of gauge forms on nonarchimedean analytic groups
gaps.detail: Defining |ω|_v on G(F_v) for a nonarchimedean local field F_v needs the F_v-analytic manifold structure of G(F_v) for smooth G and the change-of-variables formula μ(ψ(U)) = ∫_U |det Dψ|_v dμ for F_v-analytic diffeomorphisms ψ between open subsets of F_v^d. Mathlib has the inverse function theorem over complete normed fields and the real change-of-variables theorem, but not its p-adic analogue, and no layer of the atlas plans it (searched: 'analytic manifold', 'p-adic Lie', 'change of variables'). The archimedean case is covered by Mathlib's real change of variables.

gaps.title: Leading coefficient of Artin L-functions at s = 1
gaps.detail: For a connected group G whose character module X*(G_{F̄}) has nontrivial Galois action, the constant ρ_G needs the meromorphic continuation of the Artin L-function L(X, s) to a neighbourhood of s = 1 and the nonvanishing at s = 1 of L(σ, s) for the nontrivial irreducible constituents σ (Brauer induction and the nonvanishing of Hecke L-functions at s = 1). No layer of the atlas plans Artin L-functions of number fields in this generality (atlas search 'Artin L' finds only function-field and Iwasawa layers), and the libraries lack them. The split case (trivial Galois action), which covers GL_n, split tori and every semisimple group, uses only the residue of the Dedekind zeta function (Mathlib).

gaps.title: Orders of finite reductive groups (Steinberg's formula)
gaps.detail: The finite-field order estimate #𝓗(k_v)q_v^{-d}L_v(X,1)=1+O(q_v^{-2}) uniformly at good reductive places is requested from Tau Ceti ReductiveGroups layer 9, the finite-group/model owner. Its Steinberg/Bruhat/Lang proof is not supplied by the pinned libraries. GL_n and SL_n have the explicit elementary counts in this packet; the general estimate is a supplier obligation, not an adelic measure theorem.

gaps.title: Cartan's closed-subgroup theorem for p-adic analytic groups
gaps.detail: The openness of the p-adic closure of a Zariski-dense subgroup (Rapinchuk Lemma 2.7) uses Cartan's theorem that a closed subgroup of a p-adic analytic group is an analytic subgroup with a Lie algebra, together with the irreducibility of the adjoint representation of an absolutely almost simple group. Neither library has p-adic analytic groups and no atlas layer plans this theorem (searched 'Cartan', 'p-adic Lie', 'analytic group').

gaps.title: Borel density theorem
gaps.detail: Zariski density of infinite S-arithmetic subgroups of absolutely almost simple groups with G_S noncompact (Platonov–Rapinchuk Theorem 4.10, cited by Rapinchuk §2.4) is planned in no layer and absent from the libraries; Platonov–Rapinchuk is not freely available and the proof (Furstenberg's projective-measure argument) is not read here.

gaps.title: Kneser's and Harder–Chernousov's Galois-cohomology theorems
gaps.detail: Kneser's vanishing of H¹(F_v, G) for simply connected semisimple G at nonarchimedean v, the Hasse principle of Kneser–Harder–Chernousov and weak approximation for simply connected groups (Platonov–Rapinchuk Theorems 6.4, 6.6, 7.8, cited by Harpaz–Wittenberg §6) are stated here with their exact hypotheses, but their proofs (classification-based, using Bruhat–Tits theory and case-by-case work for E8) are not decomposed: the book is not freely available and no atlas layer plans the classification of simply connected groups over local and global fields.

gaps.title: Central measurable sections and character extension
gaps.detail: The exact Borel-section theorem for Polish-group homogeneous quotients, identification of the covariant completion with measurable square-integrable associated-line sections, and extension of continuous characters of closed LCA subgroups still require source-complete analytic decomposition. The density and strong-continuity proof now uses the corrected subordinate-function argument from Bekka–de la Harpe–Valette Appendix E.1; its measurable-model identification remains a separate input. The topological isomorphism X/(X∩Γ)→XΓ/Γ is not part of this gap: it follows from Mathlib’s open mapping theorem MonoidHom.isOpenMap_of_sigmaCompact (σ-compact source, locally compact target).

gaps.title: Number-field Tamagawa and Artin analytic inputs
gaps.detail: Equation (48) in Gordon is a number-field torus source, whereas Rosengarten §3 is function-field only. The canonical formula here fixes λ_v=L_v(X,1), the positive leading coefficient ρ_G, |d_F|^{-d/2}, and the additive local measures. The general finite-image Artin positive leading coefficient at s=1 and its ramified induction determinant argument still need a source-complete proof. The reductive order estimate is requested from the finite-group owner.

gaps.title: Squared-weight estimate for closed real orbits
gaps.detail: Decompose Borel–Harish-Chandra §§5.1–5.3 into the minimum-norm/Cartan squared-weight estimate and properness of the closed-orbit map modulo the stabilizer. These analytic representation lemmas are not supplied by a discrete∩compact argument or by the later adelic orbit theorem. The weight-bound node exposes this primitive input instead of using the consumer.

gaps.title: Primitive real reduction and transfer to parabolic Siegel sets
gaps.detail: Hermite–Minkowski reduction for arbitrary n, its bounded-denominator real Siegel overlap estimate, and the transfer from self-adjoint GL_n intersections to the specified parabolic domains need their full lemma proofs. The Mathlib modular-domain result proves only rank one. For disconnected groups additionally supply the compact component quotient and a Levi/semidirect covering; these are not inferred from the final class-number theorem.

gaps.title: Geometry-of-numbers height counting
gaps.detail: Supply the projective/affine number-field height-counting proof: polynomial ideal-norm counting, ideal-class representatives, a unit logarithmic fundamental domain and a uniform lattice-box count. The count node isolates those inputs; a compact height ball and discrete rational points prove finiteness but cannot prove a polynomial bound.

gaps.title: Levi extension of adelic volume and invariant-measure criterion
gaps.detail: For connected nonreductive and disconnected linear groups, prove the Levi/unipotent product integration and compact component-quotient reduction before using the general finite-volume criterion. The reductive proof and its split-centre decomposition alone do not cover these groups.

gaps.title: Real root-intersection and pivot estimates
gaps.detail: Finish the root-contraction/parabolic-normalizer lemma for intersections of deep Siegel domains (Orr–Schnell §D, Lemma 3, pp. 1234–1236), extend it to the stated distinct nonminimal parabolics, and prove the Cholesky pivot bounds in the reduced-form dictionary. The finite root-cone containment nodes do not imply these intersection estimates.

gaps.title: Arithmetic closure and anisotropic finite quotients
gaps.detail: Supply the trace-field/restriction-of-scalars Lie argument for the full S-integral group over a number field, exclude graph Lie subalgebras between distinct finite places, and eliminate arithmetic finite quotients at anisotropic compact factors. These three inputs are isolated in arithmetic-native-lie-closure and arithmetic-finite-index-elimination. Rapinchuk §2.6 reads only the ℚ single-isotropic-prime branch and refers the general proof to an uncleared book. Strong approximation itself no longer needs the graph-subalgebra or anisotropic inputs: it uses the native-field argument at one isotropic place at a time (isotropic-place-closure) and weak approximation at the anisotropic places. Those two inputs remain only for the several-place statements arithmetic-finite-product-openness and arithmetic-finite-index-elimination.

gaps.title: Obstructions to torus and non-simply-connected approximation
gaps.detail: Decompose the power-isogeny/Chebotarev obstruction for a nontrivial torus and the central-cover obstruction for a non-simply-connected absolutely almost simple group, including the finite-generation control on rational S-units. The explicit G_m/ℚ failure is verified directly; it does not establish all tori.

gaps.title: Quaternion norm topology and integral images
gaps.detail: Supply openness of the actual local reduced-norm map onto its image and its unit image at all good places, together with the integral central-cover models. These establish the restricted-product quotient homeomorphism in reduced-norm-components; a bijection of square-class sets alone does not establish it.

gaps.title: Hurwitz and Eichler concrete validation inputs
gaps.detail: Supply the norm-Euclidean argument giving class number one for the Hurwitz maximal order in (−1,−1)/ℚ, enumerate its 24 norm-one units and their 12-element effective quotient, and identify the split local Eichler unit subgroup at 3 as the stabilizer of a line in 𝔽₃², of index four. These concrete order computations are not consequences of the abstract compactness or level-mass theorem and are not yet supplied by an atlas owner.

gaps.title: Real reduction theory for reductive and disconnected groups
gaps.detail: BGST Proposition 28.1 (rational-siegel-pullback) is applied to reductive, possibly disconnected groups: an orthogonal group in BGST, and Mumford–Tate type subgroups H ⊂ SL(V) in orbit-map-siegel-preimage. Its proof needs, for such H, a covering H(ℝ) = Γ_H·C_H·𝔖_H by finitely many rational translates of one Siegel set in Orr’s convention and the Siegel property for finitely many rational translates (Borel 1969, Théorèmes 13.1 and 15.4, restated as Orr 2018, Theorems 2.2–2.3, and 15.5 as BGST cite it). The packet’s real-siegel-finite-cover and real-siegel-finite-overlap are stated only for connected semisimple G and G(ℝ)^+. The extension splits off the central ℚ-split torus, uses compactness modulo the anisotropic centre, and absorbs the finitely many components of H(ℝ), each of which meets K_H.

review.reason: BHV manuscript, Lemma E.1.3 proof, pp. 408–409: after covering the compact support by translates Ux_i the proof gives every piece the same weight f/n and bounds the error using ‖η(x) − η(x_i)‖ ≤ ε, which is known only for x in Ux_i. sourceIssues.locator: §5, p. 25 (Clay Mathematics Proceedings 4, 2005), the display relating left and right Haar measures on P(𝔸)
sourceIssues.printed: Left Haar measure on P(𝔸) is said to equal e^{2ρ_P(H_P(p))} times right Haar measure.
sourceIssues.correction: d_ℓp = e^{−2ρ_P(H_P(p))} d_rp, that is, left Haar measure is δ_P(p)^{−1} times right Haar measure.
sourceIssues.reason: For the upper triangular group of GL_2 with p = (a, u; 0, b), left multiplication rescales u by the upper-left entry and right multiplication by the lower-right entry, so left Haar measure is |a|^{−1}da* db* du (the formula Arthur himself gives on p. 21) and right Haar measure is |b|^{−1}da* db* du. Their ratio |b/a| equals e^{−2ρ(H_P(p))}, since α(H_P(p)) = log|a/b| for the unique root α and ρ = α/2.
